_comment: FALLBACK - DIAGNOSTIC ONLY. NOT IN GLSN_ITEMS. THE GATE NEVER GRADES THIS.
The shipped bench is bench/eth_chiplet_fp1505_cc.json, which attaches a real
QSPI flash device and carries NO force. This file is what that spec was until
2026-08-19: it models no flash, and it HOLDS chip_core_remap_ctrl[2] high so
CPU0's ROM fetch path can be exercised without a boot.
IT IS KEPT FOR ONE JOB: separating 'CPU0 cannot fetch from eth_rom' from
'CPU1 never released CPU0'. When the shipped bench goes red on eth_rom_port,
run this; if eth_rom_port passes here it is the handshake that broke and not
the fetch path. It runs in 8,000 cycles instead of 250,000, so it is also the
cheap way to tell a dead netlist from a slow boot.
A PASS HERE IS NOT A BOOT. It proves the eth_rom macro is reachable,
addressed and returns its firmware to a running core, and nothing else - see
the force's own `reason` field, which the generator requires and refuses to
emit without. To run it:
make -C ASIC/gls-netlist forced-fallback
which builds and runs it in its OWN directory so it cannot overwrite the
shipped item's evidence, and publishes nothing.
--- the original commentary follows ---
Bench description for the eth-chiplet pad-ring netlist. Every value here is
a name inside THIS design or a number chosen for it; none of it belongs in
the toolkit.
PROBES ARE AT THE ROM MACRO'S OWN PORT PINS, not on the AHB bus upstream.
That is deliberate: a bus-level probe can be satisfied by the testbench
itself, and the question is specifically whether a CPU reaches the macro.
CEN/A/Q at the macro boundary cannot be produced by anything but the design.
BOTH ROMs are watched in one run because the compile is the expensive step
and because the two CPUs gate each other: chip_core_remap_ctrl.v holds each
core in reset until the other writes its bootgate bit, so which core fetches
first is exactly the thing in question. chip_core_remap_ctrl_w[3:0] is that
register: bit1 = CPU1 bootgate, bit2 = CPU0 bootgate, both 0 at power-on.
The bidirectional pins carry WEAK PULLS rather than being left floating.
Nothing external drives them in this bench, and a floating inout is Z,
which is X at the first gate downstream. The design's own pad driver
still wins whenever it drives, so this models a board pull-up and not a
tie-off. Without it the boot dies of the testbench.
subs r3,#4 / ble / ldr r0,[r1,r3] / str r0,[r2,r3] / bgt, with the
destination base taken from the literal at ROM word 0x6e = 0x18000000.
memory, which is a side effect of execution and not merely a fetch.
cpu1_dmem_write is the rung-6 probe. The boot ROM's loop decodes as
subs r3,#4 / ble / ldr r0,[r1,r3] / str r0,[r2,r3] / bgt, with the
destination base from the literal at ROM word 0x6e = 0x18000000. That is
DMEM_0 per the generated linker MEMORY block - NOT IMEM, which is the
first place this probe was pointed and where it correctly saw nothing.
Watching CEN&GWEN at CPU1's DMEM macro observes the store LANDING in a
memory: a side effect of execution rather than another fetch.

forces.name: cpu0_bootgate
forces.reason: CPU0_BOOTGATE. chip_core_remap_ctrl[2] holds CPU0/eth in reset until CPU1 writes 0x4 to it, which its stage-0 bootrom only does after a QSPI XiP bring-up. This bench models no flash device, so CPU1 never reaches that write and CPU0 never fetches at all (eth_rom_port.accessed=0). Forcing the bootgate proves CPU0'S ROM FETCH PATH ONLY - that the eth_rom macro is reachable, addressed and returns its firmware to a running core. It does NOT prove the CPU1->CPU0 handshake, and a pass here must never be quoted as one. Net verified present in the fp1505 netlist: wire [3:0] chip_core_remap_ctrl_w, driven by flop u_chip_core_remap_0_remap_q_reg[2].
